Hi all,

Jeremy Avigad suggested I share this here. I have written a short expository paper for undergraduates titled "Is Math Curvy? Is Math Fat?" that investigates the geometric shape of the Lean 4 Mathlib dependency graph.

The main finding is what we call a Tree of Cliques: the graph is globally tree-like (Gromov-hyperbolic with δ = 1) yet locally dense (Jaccard-overlap proxy κ ≈ 0.022). We embed the graph into a 16-dimensional Poincaré Ball using a Hyperbolic Neural Network, then use the geometry to hunt for logical voids inside specific namespaces. Running the void-finder on the Topology namespace produces a cluster of five nearby theorems, which we feed to a language model to conjecture a unifying lemma.

The paper is intended for enthusiastic undergraduates, not as a research paper, so the methodology is deliberately accessible. Comments, corrections, and criticism are very welcome.

*Based on comments, I added a new version of the file.

Is_Math_Curvy__Is_Math_Fat (1).pdf
Hi, welcome to the Zulip chat! I have moved this post to its own thread, since it deserves more attention! :)

I wonder if the same graph properties are true of the 8/24 dim autoformalization. My hypothesis is that human-generated lemmas follow this "dense locally" pattern because of wanting to have human-friendly API around a result. This might not be the case for an autoformalized result that is "sped up" to reach the final goal.

@Ashani Dasgupta Very interesting! For a long time I've been interested in knowing non-trivial graph-theoretic properties of the Mathlib graph. Tree of Cliques is a good one!

Quick comment: "4, 40, 000 theorems" -- that's a formatting typo, I guess?

In order to remove the noise created by these high degree vertices, we prune them off
from the graph. In other words we removed the top 1% vertices (and the edges incident
on them). Suppose this new graph is M ′.

I understand why you do this. But can you give some methodological reasoning to back this up? Why 1% instead of 2% or 0.1%? Isn't this "forcing" the graph to become a tree of cliques?

I don't know anything about graph theory beyond an introductory course. So take everything I say with a wheelbarrow of salt.
I'm just a bit worried that if you take a random graph and chop off the top 1% of vertices, you are skewing your graph to become a tree of cliques.
Have you considered what happens if you, eg, remove all vertices that come from Lean core, and/or Logic/?

Note I did that kind of pruning all the way back when creating the graph at https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean-perfectoid-spaces/. But I did it by hand trying to remove only vertices that corresponded to foundations (hence are not mathematical) such as Eq or Exists. This was very imprecise, but still it tried to be something else than a generic operation turning any graph into a tree of cliques. And then I checked the obtained cliques were somewhat identifiable (those are the hand-written labels on the graph).

@Patrick Massot @Johan Commelin thank you for pointing out similar methodological concern.

I was worried about this context-blind statistical pruning as well. Maybe it is forcing the hub-dominated graph into a tree of cliques, independent of mathematical content.

I did do some computations on both the pruned and unpruned graph. I noticed the following points:

Global hyperbolicity is likely not an artefact of pruning.

I ran the Gromov δ estimator on the fully unpruned graph (619,518 nodes, 10,000 quadruples sampled, 9,997 valid, only 3 skipped). δ = 1.50 unpruned vs δ = 1.00 on pruned M′. Both confirm strong global hyperbolicity. Sample distances ranged 2–5, confirming genuine non-trivial graph structure.

Local curvature is also stable across pruning.

The curvature proxy κ ≈ 0.022 was measured on 20,000 randomly sampled edges on both graphs and remained essentially unchanged. If pruning were artificially creating clique structure, κ would shift significantly. That does not happen.

δ (Gromov): unpruned 1.50 → pruned 1.00
κ (curvature): unpruned 0.022 → pruned 0.022

To be precise: pruning cannot create cliques that weren't there. The question is whether the cliques it reveals are mathematically meaningful or generic. The κ stability suggests they are intrinsic — but the semantic pruning comparison will test this more rigorously.

That said, the semantic pruning approach is more principled than mine. Patrick's hand-removal of Eq and Exists, and Johan's suggestion of removing Lean core and Logic/ vertices, is much more mathematically meaningful. I will run this comparison explicitly.

The 1% threshold was a first pass. I agree it needs stronger justification. The formatting typo (440,000) is also fixed. Thank you!

@Yakov Pechersky this is a beautiful hypothesis. I think it's testable. If local curvature κ measures human API design choices rather than logical structure, then an autoformalized Mathlib should show κ ≈ 0 or negative. Do you know of a sufficiently large autoformalized corpus that could be used as a comparison graph?

Yes, like I mentioned above, the recently published formalization of sphere packing in 8 and 24 dimensions. That will have both human developed lemmas by the primary formalizer team and the Math Inc contributions from Gauss.

Specifically, please compare the graph topologies of the following two repos

https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean
https://github.com/math-inc/Sphere-Packing-Lean

Very nice work :octopus:

Just some trivia - "4,40,000" was presumably not a typo but the Indian decomposition of numbers (read 4 lakh 40 thousand).

@Yakov Pechersky Thank you for the pointer. This is indeed interesting. I ran a quick check. It seems, at least for this example, the autoformalization does not trim fat. Here is the data.

@Siddhartha Gadgil thank you.

As far as the typo concern, indeed, I used the Indian decomposition of number. In fact the the number is slightly incorrect. We have around 600,000 nodes as noted in the final table.

Update (March 12). Based on the feedback in this thread, I ran three null-model controls: Erdős–Rényi (matched nodes and edges), Barabási–Albert (preferential attachment with matched degree distribution), and a configuration model (Mathlib's exact degree sequence, randomly rewired). All three were pruned identically. The result: all null models have negative local curvature (κ ≈ −0.01 to −0.02), while Mathlib has κ = +0.022. The configuration model is especially striking — same degree sequence, random wiring, and κ flips from +0.022 to −0.021. This is to address @Johan Commelin's concern: pruning a hub-dominated random graph does not produce a tree of cliques. The positive curvature is specific to mathematical content.

I also extended the pipeline with an inter-domain geodesic search that detected a void between the Matroid and SimpleGraph namespaces. The LLM proposed the cycle matroid construction (Whitney 1935); the foundational definition connecting graph theory and matroid theory. I searched a bit. It seems to be absent from Mathlib (but I might be wrong). The Lean 4 formalization compiles against Mathlib v4.28.0.

The details are added in the attached file. It is now structured slightly differently from the earlier expository style to compress the relevant detail. Thank you for all the feedback. Any more criticism or feedback is much appreciated.
